catalog_quote: [p.15, 2.1 Syllable structure] In Tafi, the syllable is a tone bearing unit and it may be made up of an onset and a peak; a peak; or a peak and a coda. The onset includes any consonant that precedes the peak. The peak which always carries a tone consists of a vowel or a syllabic nasal and it is the most sonorous element in the syllable and it is also the one required component of the syllable. [...] [p.32, 2.4 Tone] Tone plays a significant role in Tafi and many other African languages. [...] The tone system of Tafi presents several complications but only the essential features of tone are discussed here. The Tafi tone system requires further investigation. In connected speech in Tafi, both level and contour tones occur. It has three level tones: Low (L), Mid (M) and High (H). new_statements.rule_in_words: Tafi is described as a tone language (three level tones L/M/H plus rising and falling contours, with lexical and grammatical functions); every syllable peak bears a tone. The grammar makes no statement at all about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be extracted from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Prosodic remarks are limited to tone (ATR/rounding harmony domains, tonal morphemes, tone changes) and to utterance-final lowered pitch in polar questions (sec. 8.2.1, pp. 244-245).
new_statements.domain_note: Only tone (syllable as TBU) and sentence-level question intonation are described; word-level stress/accent is not discussed in citation forms or phrases.
new_statements.identity_note: Bobuafor 2013 describes Tafi proper (tafi1243, autonym Tɩgbɔ), data mainly from the Mador community with some Agɔme/Abuiƒe recordings; dialect differences reported as minimal (p.8). Older sources (Funke 1910, Heine 1968, Kropp Dakubu & Ford 1988) treat Tafi together with Nyangbo/Tutrugbu (nyan1315) as 'Nyangbo-Tafi'; any stress remark found there would need checking that it is not Nyangbo-only.

new_statements.quote: [p.270, sec. 2] Tafi is a register-type tone language. In connected speech, it displays both level and contour tones. Tafi has three level tonemes: High (H), Mid (M) and Low (L) plus two complex tones, Falling (F) and Rising (R) tones which are phonetically realised on the peak of one syllable. The contour tones can be lexical or they can be generated in context as in (4b) where the falling tone could be analysed as a sequence of H and L. Tones are used for lexical contrast as in (3), and to express grammatical functions, as shown in (4). [fn. 6] The tone system of Tafi is not clear yet. [p.271] In Tafi, each syllable is a tone bearing unit.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Bobuafor 2013 (A Grammar of Tafi, ch. 2): Tafi is a three-level register tone language, the syllable is the TBU, and nothing is said about word stress. The 2009 chapter is an earlier, shorter sketch by the same author and adds nothing on stress; it agrees with the 'tone language, no stress statement' reading already recorded. The catalog's own record for Tafi carries an empty rule, which this work neither fills nor contradicts.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The chapter's only phonological sketch (sec. 2, pp. 268-271: consonants, nine-vowel ATR harmony, tone, syllable shapes, word order) describes Tafi as a register tone language with three level tonemes (H, M, L) plus falling and rising contours, tone contrasting lexical items and marking grammatical categories (e.g. present vs past progressive), with every syllable a tone-bearing unit. The words 'stress', 'prominence', 'pitch accent' do not occur anywhere in the chapter; 'accent' appears only as the name of the acute/grave tone diacritics (p. 270).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Footnote 6 (p. 270) flags that the tone system itself 'is not clear yet' and 'presents several complications which require further investigation'.
new_statements.identity_note: Bobuafor 2009 describes Tafi (autonym Tɩgbɔ, people Bagbɔ) as spoken in the four communities Agɔme, Madɔ, Abuiƒé and Atome in the Volta Region of Ghana, c. 4,400 speakers; no particular dialect is singled out. The chapter notes mutual intelligibility with neighbouring Nyagbo (a separate languoid) but its data are Tafi only.

sources.note: Nothing. Ch. 2 Phonology (pp. 15-50) covers syllable structure, consonants, vowels/ATR harmony, tone (2.4: three level tones L/M/H plus contours, lexical and grammatical function), processes, loanwords, orthography; the syllable is defined as the tone-bearing unit whose peak 'always carries a tone' (p.15). No section or sentence on word stress/accent anywhere in the book (whole text searched via decoded text layer; only hits are 'distress', 'stresses the point', and 'acute/grave accent' as tone diacritics). Polar questions marked by lowered final pitch (p.244-245).
